title: What to Do When a Parent Refuses Hospice
seoTitle: When a Parent Refuses Hospice: A Family Guide
description: When a parent refuses hospice, steady conversation and practical questions can help. Learn how to listen, revisit care goals, and support choice.
lede: When a parent says no to hospice, the answer can feel like a closed door. You may be watching symptoms, falls, hospital visits, or exhaustion while they hear hospice as a loss of hope. Your task is not to win an argument. It is to understand what the word means to them, offer accurate information, and keep the relationship safe enough for another conversation.

sections.heading: Start with the fear beneath the refusal
paragraphs: A refusal often protects something important. Your parent may fear that hospice means giving up, losing a personal physician, being moved from home, or having every decision taken away. They may worry about money, medications, religion, or what an enrollment conversation says about the future. Ask gently: “What concerns you most when you hear hospice?” Then listen without correcting the first sentence. A pause is not agreement; it is room for trust.

Reflect what you heard before offering information: “You want to stay in your apartment and remain in charge. That makes sense.” This does not mean you have solved every concern. It shows that you are taking the person, not just the care plan, seriously. If conversations become heated, stop and return later rather than turning a deeply personal decision into a family vote.

sections.heading: Use questions instead of pressure
paragraphs: Try replacing “You need hospice” with questions about goals. What would make home feel safer? Which symptoms are hardest? What matters most in the next few weeks or months? Who should be involved in decisions? A parent may be more willing to discuss help with comfort, bathing, equipment, or caregiver strain than to discuss the label hospice. Those practical needs can reveal where a conversation with the care team would help.

Avoid threats, guilt, and predictions you cannot know. “If you loved us, you would do this” can make a person withdraw. So can promising that hospice will fix everything. Hospice is a service option, not a guarantee of a particular timeline or outcome. Eligibility is individualized and requires physician certification; an information visit can explain whether it may fit without forcing enrollment.

sections.heading: Invite a calm, factual conversation
paragraphs: Ask the parent’s physician or another trusted clinician to describe the current situation in plain language. You can request a family meeting, with your parent’s permission, and prepare a short list of questions. Ask what changes the clinician is seeing, what treatments are still available, what burdens they bring, and what support exists at home. Ask how hospice would work alongside the person’s goals and who makes the final decision.

A hospice information visit can be educational. The family can ask about team members, visits, equipment, medications related to the terminal illness, after-hours processes, and caregiver support. Ask the provider to explain coverage and any possible patient costs in writing. Medicare and other plans have specific rules; never assume every service or medication is covered.

sections.heading: Protect autonomy while planning safety
paragraphs: An adult with decision-making capacity has the right to accept or decline care, even when family members disagree. You can still help make the current plan safer. Write down the preferred number to call, medication instructions from the clinician, fall-prevention steps, and signs that require urgent medical attention. Clarify who can speak with clinicians and whether an advance directive or health care proxy is current.

If you are unsure about capacity, do not try to settle that question during a family argument. Ask the treating clinician for guidance. A refusal made while confused, severely distressed, or unable to understand information deserves prompt clinical attention. In an emergency—such as severe breathing difficulty, uncontrolled bleeding, a serious fall, or a sudden change in awareness—call emergency services unless a documented plan says otherwise.

sections.heading: Keep the door open
paragraphs: People change their minds as symptoms, goals, or circumstances change. Set a specific time to revisit the conversation: after the next appointment, after a hospital discharge, or if caregiving becomes unsafe. Keep a simple log of symptoms, sleep, appetite, falls, urgent calls, and what helps. The log is not an argument; it gives the family and clinicians a clearer picture.

You can say, “I will respect your decision today, and I would like us to keep talking if your needs change.” A hospice team can answer questions even before a decision. In Ventura and Los Angeles Counties, families may want to compare how agencies respond, coordinate with physicians, and support care in a home, facility, or other setting.

If your parent remains unsure, offer a smaller next step. Ask permission to call for an information visit, invite a trusted relative to join, or write down questions for the next appointment. You can also ask what kind of help would feel acceptable today. Respectful persistence is different from pressure: it keeps support visible while allowing the person to make an informed choice. Revisit the plan whenever the person’s wishes or needs change.

ctaHeading: A conversation can begin without a decision
ctaCopy: If hospice is being discussed, Eternal Life Hospice can provide a clear, no-pressure conversation about goals, support, and next steps. Call 805.953.7273.

title: How to Choose a Hospice Provider
seoTitle: How to Choose a Hospice Provider | Family Guide
description: Compare hospice providers with practical questions about care, communication, coverage, and local support for families in Ventura and Los Angeles Counties.
lede: Choosing a hospice is both a practical decision and a deeply personal one. The right provider should make the plan understandable, respect the patient’s goals, and communicate clearly with everyone involved. Families in Ventura and Los Angeles Counties can compare providers before a crisis, even if a hospital or facility has already offered a referral.

sections.heading: Begin with fit, not a sales pitch
paragraphs: Ask each provider to explain how care would look for this person, in this setting, with these priorities. Hospice is generally delivered where the person lives—such as a private home, assisted-living community, or skilled-nursing facility—rather than requiring a move. A provider should explain what the team can do, what it cannot do, and who remains responsible for decisions.

Look for calm, specific answers. “We are here 24/7” should mean an on-call clinician can be reached at any hour, not that a nurse will be continuously at the bedside. Ask how urgent concerns are triaged, how quickly in-person visits can be arranged when clinically indicated, and how the team communicates after a change.

sections.heading: Check credentials and clinical structure
paragraphs: Confirm that the organization is licensed and Medicare-certified if that coverage matters to your family, and ask about accreditation without treating a logo as the whole answer. Request the names or roles of the attending physician, hospice medical director, nurse, social worker, spiritual care professional, and aides who may participate. Ask how the plan is created and updated.

Ask whether the patient’s own physician can remain involved and how orders are coordinated. Eligibility is individualized and physician-certified; a provider should not promise acceptance before reviewing the clinical picture. Ask how recertification and changes in status are handled, using plain language rather than predictions.

When comparing providers, ask how they welcome feedback from patients and families. A short follow-up after the first visit can reveal whether instructions were understood and whether the plan fits real life. Keep the patient’s voice central, especially when relatives disagree. If the family needs more time, say so plainly and ask what information would make the next conversation useful.

sections.heading: Ask about the everyday experience
paragraphs: Who will be the main contact? How often does a nurse typically visit, and what factors change that schedule? How are personal care needs assessed? What equipment can be arranged, and who delivers or maintains it? What happens if the patient moves between home, a facility, hospital, or another county? These questions help reveal whether the provider has a workable local network.

Ask how the provider supports caregivers. A social worker may help with planning, resources, and emotional support; spiritual care is offered according to the patient’s wishes. In-home hospice is not the same as round-the-clock private-duty caregiving. Families should understand what they will still need to arrange and what respite options may be available under the benefit and the patient’s plan.

sections.heading: Understand costs and coverage
paragraphs: Request a written explanation of what the patient’s insurance or benefit covers and what may involve cost sharing. Under the Medicare Hospice Benefit, covered services related to the terminal illness are generally covered without a deductible for the hospice benefit itself, but some comfort medications may have a small copayment and inpatient respite can involve coinsurance. Coverage details vary.

Ask who handles medications, equipment, and supplies, and what happens when an item is unrelated to the terminal illness. Do not assume that every complementary or integrative activity is a Medicare-covered hospice service. Ask whether it is available as an optional comfort offering, who provides it, and whether there is a charge.

sections.heading: Notice communication and respect
paragraphs: During an initial call, notice whether staff ask about the patient’s wishes or speak only to the family. A good conversation makes room for culture, language, gender identity, family structure, pets, work schedules, and spiritual practices without stereotyping. Ask how concerns are documented and escalated, and how a family can request a change in team member or revisit the plan.

Compare two or three providers when time allows, but do not delay urgent support while collecting a perfect list. Hospitals, facilities, physicians, friends, and community organizations can offer names; the family is generally free to choose a hospice that participates with the patient’s coverage. You can change providers later if the fit is not right, following the applicable process.

It can help to create a comparison sheet with the provider name, main contact, service area, response process, team structure, caregiver support, coverage explanation, and questions still unanswered. Ask for references only when appropriate and protect patient privacy. The best choice is not necessarily the largest organization or the one that calls first; it is the provider whose plan is clear, available, culturally responsive, and aligned with the patient’s wishes.

title: Questions to Ask a Doctor About Hospice
seoTitle: Questions to Ask Your Doctor About Hospice
description: A practical list of questions helps families discuss hospice, comfort goals, timing, coverage, and next steps with a trusted physician and care team.
lede: A hospice conversation with a doctor does not need to be a single, dramatic question. It can be a structured discussion about what is changing, what matters most, and what support could make the coming months more manageable. Bring this list to an appointment, hospital meeting, or care conference, and invite the patient to lead where possible.

sections.heading: Ask for an honest picture
paragraphs: Start with: “What changes are you seeing, and what should we expect next?” Ask the doctor to explain the condition, likely course, uncertainty, and warning signs in everyday language. You can ask, “Would you be surprised if this person were living six months from now?” That is not a request for a guarantee; it is a way to understand whether hospice evaluation is appropriate.

Ask what is reversible and what is not, which tests or treatments would change the plan, and what burdens they may bring. Hospice is considered when a physician certifies an individualized prognosis consistent with the benefit’s rules, but only the clinical team can assess this person.

sections.heading: Clarify goals and options
paragraphs: Ask, “What would comfort-focused care look like now?” and “Which hospital visits or procedures might be avoidable if symptoms are managed at home?” Discuss whether the priority is staying at home, attending a family event, maintaining alertness, reducing distress, or another goal. Goals can change, and the plan can be revisited.

Ask whether palliative care, home health, disease-directed treatment, hospice, or another service is the best fit at this moment. These services differ. A clinician should explain what remains available and what would change if hospice begins. No family should feel that asking about hospice means refusing every form of medical attention.

Write down the doctor’s recommendations in the patient’s own words. Ask which changes should trigger a call today, this week, or at the next visit. A family may also ask whether a hospice information visit can happen at home, in a facility, or by another appropriate arrangement. The purpose is understanding; enrollment is a separate choice made after the evaluation and discussion.

sections.heading: Understand who does what
paragraphs: Ask how the physician will work with the hospice medical director and team. Can the patient’s doctor remain involved? Who writes orders? Who answers after hours? What happens on weekends? Clarify that 24/7 support means access to an on-call hospice professional for questions and urgent guidance; it does not mean continuous bedside nursing.

Ask what visits are typical from nurses, aides, social workers, spiritual care professionals, and volunteers. Ask how care is coordinated with a facility or home caregivers. Knowing roles early prevents disappointment and helps the family plan transportation, medication pickup, meals, and supervision.

sections.heading: Discuss symptoms, medications, and equipment
paragraphs: Ask what symptoms should prompt a call, which signs require emergency services, and what comfort plan will be available. Ask how prescriptions are coordinated and which medications relate to the terminal illness. Never change or stop a medication without guidance from the treating clinician or hospice team.

Ask whether the patient may need a hospital bed, oxygen, commode, wheelchair, or other equipment, who supplies it, and how quickly. Discuss allergies, preferred pharmacy, language access, and who can receive instructions. If the patient lives in assisted living or skilled nursing, ask how the facility and hospice share updates.

sections.heading: Bring the practical questions
paragraphs: Ask how eligibility is reviewed, what coverage applies, and what costs could remain. Medicare coverage details can include limited cost sharing for certain comfort medications or inpatient respite; plans vary, so request a benefits explanation. Ask whether services outside the hospice plan, including optional comfort activities, involve separate arrangements or charges.

Finish with: “What are the next two steps, and who will call whom?” A physician can send a referral for an informational visit, with the patient’s permission. Write down the doctor’s answers, names, and phone numbers. A clear plan lowers anxiety even when the family is not ready to enroll.

If emotions take over the appointment, ask for a second meeting or invite a social worker to join. The patient can request an interpreter rather than relying on a child or relative for medical translation. Ask for written instructions and repeat back the plan: “Here is what we will do today; here is who we call if things change.” Good questions are not a challenge to the physician. They are a way to make shared decisions safer and more understandable.

You can ask the doctor to document the plan in the medical record and share it with the authorized caregivers. This is especially useful when several relatives, a facility, and a specialist are involved. A written plan does not remove uncertainty, but it gives everyone the same starting point and makes it easier to notice when the patient’s goals have changed.

ctaHeading: Bring your questions; we will bring clarity
ctaCopy: Eternal Life Hospice can speak with families and clinicians about a possible hospice evaluation. Call 805.953.7273 for a straightforward conversation.

title: Eating and Drinking Changes Near the End of Life
seoTitle: Eating and Drinking Changes Near the End of Life
description: Learn how appetite and thirst may change near the end of life, how to offer comfort safely, and when to call the care team for guidance and support.
lede: Eating and drinking can carry enormous emotional weight. Food may represent love, family, strength, and routine, so a smaller appetite can be frightening. Near the end of life, the body may need and tolerate less. A person’s care team can help you distinguish comfort from pressure, protect safety, and honor preferences without turning every bite into a test.

sections.heading: Understand the change without blaming yourself
paragraphs: Reduced appetite, longer pauses, and less interest in fluids can occur as illness advances. A person may sleep more, tire quickly, or find familiar foods unappealing. This is not a simple matter of willpower, and forcing food can lead to distress, coughing, nausea, or conflict. Ask the physician or hospice nurse what they are seeing in this individual rather than relying on a general timeline.

Families often feel they are failing when a loved one eats less. You are not responsible for making someone eat. Your presence, a calm voice, mouth care, music, a hand to hold, or a favorite scent may express love just as clearly as a meal.

The goal is not to meet a nutritional target at all costs. It is to notice comfort, dignity, and connection. A clinician can help you understand what is happening and make a plan that fits the person’s wishes, culture, and safety.

sections.heading: Let comfort guide the offer
paragraphs: Offer small amounts without pressure: a spoonful of a favorite flavor, an ice chip if approved, or a sip when the person is awake and interested. Keep the person upright and allow plenty of time. Stop when they turn away, cough, tire, or show discomfort. Ask what feels good today; preferences can change from morning to evening.

Do not introduce new supplements, thickened liquids, or feeding techniques without professional guidance. Swallowing ability can change, and a clinician may recommend a safer approach. If the person has a diet or fluid restriction for another condition, ask the care team how that fits with comfort-focused goals.

Caregivers can also ask how to balance visits with rest and privacy. A person may want company one day and quiet the next. Tell the team about cultural food practices, favorite drinks, dentures, and past swallowing problems. These details help the plan reflect the person rather than a generic checklist. When in doubt, pause the offer and ask the nurse for individualized guidance.

sections.heading: Make mouth care a priority
paragraphs: Dry mouth can feel uncomfortable even when the person does not want to drink. Ask the nurse to demonstrate gentle mouth care and discuss appropriate swabs, a soft toothbrush, lip moisturizer, and denture care. Keep the mouth clean and moist according to the care plan, taking care not to pour liquid into a mouth that cannot safely swallow.

Mouth care is also a moment of connection. Explain what you are doing, move slowly, and respect a person who says no. If the mouth looks painful, has sores, bleeds, or develops a new coating or odor, tell the clinical team. The team can assess the cause and recommend comfort measures.

sections.heading: Know when to call
paragraphs: Call the hospice team for new coughing with sips, choking, repeated vomiting, pain, agitation, a swollen abdomen, markedly reduced urination, or any change that worries you. The on-call team can offer guidance at any hour. 24/7 on-call support is not continuous bedside nursing, so ask what to do while help is being arranged.

Call emergency services for an immediate life-threatening emergency unless the patient’s documented plan directs otherwise. If the family is unsure whether a change is expected, calling early is appropriate. Keep the care team’s number visible and tell every caregiver where it is.

sections.heading: Talk about feeding decisions with care
paragraphs: Some families ask about feeding tubes or IV fluids when eating declines. Those decisions depend on the person’s condition, goals, ability to swallow, risks, and informed preferences. Ask the physician to explain potential benefits, burdens, and alternatives in this specific case. A hospice team can support a goals-of-care conversation; it should not pressure the family toward a predetermined answer.

Focus on what the person can enjoy and tolerate now. A favorite song during mouth care, a familiar cup, a cool cloth, or a quiet visit may bring comfort. If the person is able to speak, follow their lead. If they cannot, use known wishes and the authorized decision-maker, with clinical guidance.

Families sometimes interpret less intake as a sign that they should keep offering more. Instead, watch the person’s cues and ask the clinical team how to respond. A quiet room, loose clothing, gentle positioning, and regular lip care may be more welcome than a full tray. If the person is alert and wants a favorite food, enjoying a small amount can be meaningful even when nutrition is no longer the main goal. Comfort and dignity remain the guide.

ctaHeading: You do not have to navigate this alone
ctaCopy: For practical guidance about appetite, swallowing, and comfort, call Eternal Life Hospice at 805.953.7273. Our team can help you know what to ask next.

title: Grief Support Before and After a Loss
seoTitle: Grief Support Before and After a Loss
description: Grief can begin before a death and continue long afterward. Learn how families can prepare, ask for support, and care for themselves through change.
lede: Grief does not begin on a predictable date, and it does not follow a straight line. Families may feel sorrow, anger, relief, numbness, gratitude, or several emotions in one afternoon. When someone is seriously ill, grief can begin before the death as roles, routines, and hopes change. Thoughtful support makes room for the whole experience before and after a loss.

sections.heading: Name the grief that is already here
paragraphs: Anticipatory grief may arise when a diagnosis, decline, or new care role changes family life. You may grieve a future, a shared activity, independence, or the way a relationship used to feel. Naming this does not mean you are giving up on the person. It means you are responding to a real change while continuing to show up.

Try a simple check-in: “What has been hardest this week?” The answer may be practical rather than emotional—sleep, transportation, finances, or conflict among relatives. Support should address the whole family’s situation. A hospice social worker or spiritual care professional can listen, help with resources, and respect the family’s beliefs.

sections.heading: Make room for honest conversations
paragraphs: Ask the ill person what matters most, what they fear, who should be present, and what they would like remembered. Do not force a final conversation or insist on closure. A shared meal, a photograph, a favorite story, or quiet company may be enough. Follow the person’s energy and preferences.

Families do not need perfect words. “I love you,” “I am here,” and “You do not have to take care of my feelings right now” can be meaningful. If conflict is longstanding, focus on safety and the person’s wishes rather than trying to repair every history at the bedside.

Grief support should not require you to explain or defend every feeling. A trusted person can simply listen and help you notice what you need. If you are caring for someone who is still living, ask the team how to share your grief without placing emotional weight on that person. Boundaries, rest, and outside support can protect the relationship while allowing honest feelings.

sections.heading: Prepare for the practical side
paragraphs: Before a death, ask the care team what changes to expect, whom to call, and what paperwork or cultural practices matter. Identify the decision-maker, keep contact information current, and tell relatives how updates will be shared. A plan can reduce frantic decisions while still leaving room for the unexpected.

After a death, practical tasks arrive when concentration may be low. Ask a trusted person to help with calls, meals, children, pets, and paperwork. Hospice bereavement staff can explain available support and how to access community resources. Support varies by provider and circumstance, so ask what is offered and for how long.

sections.heading: Care for the body carrying grief
paragraphs: Grief can affect sleep, appetite, focus, and energy. Choose small, doable care: drink water, step outside, take prescribed medications as directed, accept a meal, or ask someone to sit with you. You do not have to be productive to be grieving well. A few steady routines can provide a gentle anchor.

Reach out if sadness, fear, anger, or numbness feels unmanageable, lasts in a concerning way, or affects safety. A primary care clinician, licensed mental-health professional, faith leader, support group, or crisis service may help. If someone may hurt themselves or cannot stay safe, call emergency services or a crisis line immediately.

sections.heading: Remember that there is no single right way
paragraphs: One family member may want to talk; another may want quiet. One person may return to work quickly; another may need more time. Culture, age, relationship, prior losses, and circumstances all shape grief. Avoid comparing timelines or judging a reaction as too much or too little.

Anniversaries and ordinary moments can bring grief back sharply. Keep a ritual that feels authentic: lighting a candle, cooking a recipe, visiting a meaningful place, or telling a story. Connection does not erase loss. It can help the relationship continue in a changed form.

Children and teenagers grieve too, even when adults try to protect them from difficult information. Use clear, age-appropriate words and avoid euphemisms that can confuse them. Tell them what will stay the same, invite questions, and let them choose a safe way to participate. Schools, counselors, pediatric clinicians, and grief programs may help. Do not make a child responsible for an adult’s emotional or practical care; give them dependable adults and honest reassurance.

After a loss, practical grief can be overlooked: a quieter home, changed finances, new responsibilities, or the absence of the person who handled daily tasks. Make a list of what must happen now and what can wait. Accept help with specific tasks, and allow yourself to learn unfamiliar routines slowly. There is no deadline for becoming comfortable with a changed life.

ctaHeading: Support is part of compassionate care
ctaCopy: Eternal Life Hospice offers families a place to ask about grief and bereavement support before and after a loss. Call 805.953.7273 to connect.

title: How Physicians and Facilities Refer a Patient to Hospice
seoTitle: How Physicians and Facilities Refer to Hospice
description: A clear hospice referral supports timely, coordinated care. Learn what physicians and facilities can send, what families decide, and what happens next.
lede: A hospice referral is a clinical handoff and a human conversation. Physicians, hospitals, skilled-nursing facilities, and assisted-living communities often recognize when a patient and family need more support, but may wonder what information to send or how quickly an evaluation can occur. A clear process respects patient choice while helping the team respond without avoidable delay.

sections.heading: Start with goals and permission
paragraphs: Ask the patient—or the legally authorized decision-maker when appropriate—whether they want hospice information. Explain that a referral requests an evaluation and conversation; it does not enroll someone automatically. Share the patient’s goals, preferred setting, decision-maker, language needs, and the concerns prompting the referral.

A referral should never be used to pressure a patient. Eligibility is individualized and requires physician certification under applicable rules. The hospice evaluates the clinical picture, confirms coverage and location, and discusses options with the patient and family. The patient retains the right to choose a provider and to accept or decline care.

sections.heading: Send the clinical picture
paragraphs: Useful records commonly include the referral order or request, relevant diagnoses and history, recent notes, medication list, allergies, recent hospital or emergency visits, test results that inform the picture, functional changes, symptom concerns, and contact information for treating clinicians. Include the patient’s current location and anticipated discharge date when timing matters.

Share what has changed: increasing assistance with daily activities, repeated infections or hospitalizations, weight or intake concerns, falls, wounds, worsening symptoms, or a shift in goals. Avoid relying on a diagnosis code alone. A concise narrative helps the hospice clinician understand the person behind the chart.

When a referral is sent, confirm receipt rather than assuming the fax or electronic message arrived. Ask who will contact the family and by what time. If the patient’s condition changes while the evaluation is pending, update the hospice and treating clinician. Prompt, complete communication reduces duplicate questions and helps the patient receive the right kind of attention at the right time.

sections.heading: Coordinate across settings
paragraphs: For a hospital discharge, identify who will be with the patient, what equipment is needed, which medications are due, and when the patient will arrive. For a skilled-nursing or assisted-living referral, identify facility contacts, medication administration procedures, emergency protocols, and family communication preferences. Confirm that orders and records move through the approved secure channel.

Hospice and facility teams should clarify who responds after hours, how urgent changes are escalated, and when updates return to the referring clinician. On-call support is available 24/7 for hospice patients, but it does not mean continuous bedside nursing. Clear expectations protect staff, patients, and families.

sections.heading: Explain the evaluation to the family
paragraphs: Families may be worried that a referral means treatment stops or that they will lose their physician. Explain that hospice focuses on comfort and quality of life while coordinating with the care team; the patient’s personal physician may remain involved depending on the plan. The hospice can describe team roles, visits, equipment, medications, caregiver support, and what happens if needs change.

Coverage should be discussed accurately. Medicare and other plans have specific requirements and possible cost sharing. Do not promise that services are free or that every medication, supply, or integrative modality is covered. Invite the family to ask for a written explanation and to confirm details with the hospice and plan.

sections.heading: Close the loop
paragraphs: Document that the patient or authorized decision-maker agreed to an information visit or referral, along with preferences and outstanding questions. Give the family a named contact. After the hospice evaluation, confirm whether the patient enrolled, chose another provider, deferred the decision, or needs a different service. Respect privacy and share only what is appropriate and authorized.

If the patient is not eligible now, ask what changes should prompt a new referral and what supportive services fit meanwhile. If the patient enrolls, send updated orders and participate in care-plan communication as agreed. A referral is successful when the patient’s goals are understood and the next step is clear—not merely when a form is transmitted.

Facilities can improve continuity by naming a referral champion, using a consistent checklist, and reviewing delayed or incomplete referrals at team meetings. Include the family’s preferred contact method and the patient’s communication needs in the handoff. When a referral is urgent, say why and identify the deadline. A brief call between clinicians can clarify a complex situation, while secure records provide the details needed for a safe evaluation.

Keep the referral focused on the patient’s needs, not only on a prognosis estimate. Include what the patient says matters, what the family can manage, and what support is missing. Those details help the hospice team prepare a respectful conversation and identify questions that need the referring clinician’s input. A complete handoff is an act of care.

ctaCopy: Eternal Life Hospice partners with physicians and facilities across Ventura and Los Angeles Counties. Call 805.953.7273 to discuss a referral or request an information visit.
